title: Growing the practice
summary: Where more revenue can come from in a facility-based practice, in order of safety: stop the leaks, bill what patients already qualify for, add clinician capacity, add sites, then add contracts. With the arithmetic for each.

blocks.text: Revenue in a visiting practice is arithmetic. Growth means changing one of the terms, and each term has a different cost and a different risk.

blocks.label: Revenue
blocks.expr: (clinicians x working days x visits per day x collected per visit) + (patients in monthly programs x collected per patient-month) + stipends - leakage

blocks.text: Two rules of thumb fall out of those numbers. Every ten additional residents under care are worth about $13,000 to $19,000 a year at today's payments. The figure reaches $31,000 only if care management is paid for every resident every month. And the cheapest growth available is the last line: money already earned and not collected.
Before adding a single patient, the practice can collect more from the patients it has. None of this needs a new clinician, a new site or a new contract.

blocks.title: Why this comes first
blocks.text: Leak repair is nearly all margin and carries no compliance risk. It also makes every later lever worth more, because new volume poured into a leaky process leaks at the same rate.

sections.heading: Lever 2: services your patients already qualify for

blocks.text: Medicare pays for several services that fit long-term residents and that this practice is not billing, or is billing in a way that needs repair.

blocks.text: The honest size of this lever is modest: about a dozen wellness visits a month and a few transitional care services, worth about $21,000 to $41,000 a year. The larger number sits in care management: about $165,000 a year at October's volume and today's paid rate, and about $370,000 if every line were paid.

blocks.title: Growth that destroys value
blocks.text: A new service adds value only when each claim meets its rule. Otherwise the money is denied, or paid and later taken back. A wellness visit repeated within 12 months is denied. Advance care planning with no minutes in the note can be denied in full. Transitional care is not payable when the patient goes to a nursing facility. Write the template and the checklist for each service before the first claim goes out.

blocks.q: A patient goes from the hospital to a skilled nursing facility. Can transitional care management be billed?
choices: No. It applies to discharges to a community setting such as home or assisted living
blocks.why: The service is for the return to a community setting. Your nursing facility visit is billed with nursing facility codes.

blocks.text: With leaks fixed, clinician time is the limit. A nurse practitioner is the usual next hire in this kind of practice.

rows: Median pay, primary care nurse practitioner
Pay with payroll tax, benefits, malpractice and tools
Visits a day to cover cost

items: Medicare pays a nurse practitioner 85% of the physician rate, and the figures above already reflect that.

Enrollment takes time. Medicare processes most clean online applications within 15 to 50 days, and each plan adds its own wait. Start the day the offer is signed, and budget three months before full billing.
In a skilled nursing facility the physician must still personally do the required comprehensive visit and alternate the required visits, so one physician can support only so many nurse practitioners.
Florida allows a nurse practitioner with 3,000 supervised hours to register for autonomous practice in primary care. That removes the supervision protocol, not the Medicare rules.

blocks.text: The hire also does something a spreadsheet does not show: it moves visits and relationships away from the owner, which is the main thing a buyer or a lender wants to see.

blocks.q: A new nurse practitioner sees 9 patients a day for her first four months. What is happening to profit?
choices: It falls until she passes about 12 visits a day and her enrollments are active
blocks.why: Below break-even volume, and before enrollments are active, a new clinician costs more than she collects. Plan cash for the ramp.

blocks.text: A new facility is worth adding when it brings enough residents to justify the trip. The questions are the same every time.

items: How many residents would be under the practice's care in the first three months, and at maturity?
Who decides physician coverage there, and why would they change?
Is it on an existing route, or does it add an hour of driving?
Which clinician will go, on which days, and what stops if they do?
What does the facility expect in return: response times, family meetings, a medical director?

blocks.text: At about $1,300 to $1,900 a year per resident, it takes roughly 105 to 150 residents under care to equal one nurse practitioner's cost, so a new site usually fills an existing clinician's day before it justifies a hire.

blocks.title: Concentration cuts both ways
blocks.text: One hospital is 37.8% of this practice's charges. Hospital work pays well per visit but depends on a referral pattern the practice does not control. Growth that lowers the share of the largest site is worth more than the same dollars added to it.

items: Medical directorships

Every nursing facility must have a physician medical director. The stipend must be fair market value for documented work, under a written agreement, and unrelated to referrals. Keep a time log. Stipends here fell from $185,300 in 2023 to about $32,000 a year.
Special needs plans for nursing home residents
These Medicare Advantage plans need clinicians on site and often pay for availability and outcomes as well as visits.
Accountable care organizations
Joining one can bring shared savings and satisfies some quality reporting. Medicare's new accountable care model starts in 2027.
Hospice and home health
They need attending physicians for facility patients. Any payment to you must be for real services at fair market value.
Payer rates
Small volumes limit bargaining power, but a local plan that needs coverage in nursing facilities may pay above Medicare. You cannot ask without knowing your current rates.

blocks.title: The line you cannot cross
blocks.text: Nothing of value may be given or received in exchange for referrals of Medicare or Medicaid patients. That covers stipends above fair market value, free services to a facility, and gifts to case managers. Have the attorney read any arrangement with an entity that sends you patients.

items: **Cash.** Medicare pays in about 18 days here, plans in 30 to 45. A new clinician or site is paid for by the practice for two to four months before it pays back. Cash on hand is 48 days.
**Oversight.** Every new clinician needs a chart audit in the first 90 days. Patterns set early are hard to change later.
**Enrollment and contracts.** Each clinician with each payer, tracked on one calendar.
**Your time.** Growth that needs more of the owner makes the key-person problem worse.

takeaways: Fix leakage first: it is nearly all margin and makes every other lever worth more.
Every ten additional residents under care are worth about $13,000 to $19,000 a year at today's payments. The figure reaches $31,000 only if care management is paid for every resident every month.
A nurse practitioner covers her cost at about 12 visits a day. Profit starts above that, after a ramp of several months.
A monthly program is worth what gets paid. Care management is paid on about 42% of lines today.
Prefer growth that lowers dependence on the owner and on the largest site.
Never trade anything of value for referrals.
